basing-tips.name: Jungle floor
basing-tips.summary: Dark damp earth in mixed browns, leaf litter and plants, with green creeping over it all
materials: Clumpy texture paste, or grit mixed into white glue and filler
White glue thinned with a little water
Very fine green scatter and grit in two sizes
Loose tea leaves crumbled small, for leaf litter
Tufts, paper ferns or cut down aquarium plants
A little green brown pigment for dry patches
howto: Spread clumpy paste over the base without worrying about gaps, and push the feet in while it's soft.
Brush on watery glue and sprinkle fine green scatter rather than grass, then grit and crumbled tea as leaf litter.
Glue plants on before priming, leaving room for the feet, and varnish after priming to lock loose bits.
Wash green over the brown and brown over the green, always pooling it round the foot of each plant.
Dot thin purple brown in low spots as wet mud and dust pigment on dry patches, so the earth shows several browns.

paintSteps.note: Brown round the edge with a deep green down the middle, as the jungle floor gets little light.
Lightly over everything, the plants most, to pick out their texture.
Dabbed into the green and over into the brown, as moss and mud run together.
Over the brown and the plant stems, so packet plants stop looking fake.
Along leaf edges with the side of the brush, where a slip just looks natural.

basing-tips.name: Graveyard
basing-tips.summary: Muddy grave earth round a weathered headstone, with rain puddles and a few tufts
materials: A spare headstone, or one cut from plastic card
Fine garden soil, baked dry and sieved
Epoxy putty and thin super glue
Clear gloss gel or water effect with a little green tint
Grass tufts
A spare skull or hand, if you like
howto: Cut a headstone from plastic card, sand the edges, and add a small cross or trim if you want.
Fix the stone with putty, pressing a low mound in front of it for the grave itself.
Cover the base in sieved soil and soak it with thin super glue, which sets it hard as stone.
Once painted, pour tinted gloss into the dips in thin layers for rain puddles, as it shrinks while drying.
Glue a few tufts at the foot of the stone and paint the rim black.

paintSteps.note: The headstone.
Dabbed on the stone for wear and grime.
Rough, scratchy edges so the stone looks old.
The grave earth, with a lighter brown drybrush over the top.

basing-tips.name: Muddy trench
basing-tips.summary: A plank lined trench wall and duckboards sunk in churned mud
materials: Quick setting epoxy putty for the trench wall
Coffee stirrers, matchsticks or thin frame plastic strips for planks
Thick mud texture paint or paste
Fine garden soil, sieved
Gloss varnish for puddles
A few grass tufts
howto: Build up a low wall of putty along one side, working fast and wearing gloves, as it sets quickly.
Face the wall with planks and lay short strips across the floor as duckboards, nicking the wood for damage.
Push thick mud into every gap, slope it down to the rim and part bury a plank end or two.
Tint a few planks with thin red, green or yellow filters so the wood doesn't read as one board.
Gloss the hollows for puddles, then brush thinned mud over the tufts so they look trampled.

paintSteps.note: On the planks and duckboards.
The wood colour mixed half and half with white.
On every third plank, or the top half of one, for variety.
Over the lower planks where mud splashes up.

basing-tips.name: River bed
basing-tips.summary: Rounded pebbles under clear water, deep blue in the middle and paler at the banks
materials: Rocks or bark chunks for the banks
Leftover putty rolled into pebbles, or small real stones
Fine sand and white glue
Dark blue, murky green and sandy tan paints
Gloss varnish, or clear water resin for depth
Grass tufts for the banks
howto: Glue rocks along the banks and fill the bed with smooth rounded pebbles, with sand between them.
Real stones look natural unpainted under clear water, but paint any that sit on the dry bank.
Paint the bed dark blue and, while it's wet, blend murky green and brown into the middle.
Stipple thinned tan out from each bank into the water so it looks shallower at the edges.
Gloss it, or pour clear resin in thin layers with a little tint in a middle layer, then add tufts.

paintSteps.note: Slightly thinned so it spreads easily over the stones.
Into the middle while the blue is wet, away from the banks.
About half water, stippled from the bank inwards.
Makes it read as wet and hides blotchy blending.

basing-tips.name: Autumn leaf litter
basing-tips.summary: Fallen leaves in brown, red and gold over dark earth, with faded grass and a twig
materials: Fine soil or dark sand, white glue and water
Dried birch seeds or leaf scatter
Small twigs or lichen covered roots
Golden or straw coloured tufts
Grass fibres and a little matte varnish
Tweezers
howto: Paint the bare base dark brown, then spread on soil, glue and water mixed in equal parts.
Press twigs and a stone or two into the wet paste and leave it at least an hour.
Varnish any green grass fibres so they stiffen, then repaint them in faded, yellowed greens.
Sprinkle leaves onto a layer of white glue, or set single ones with tweezers, and tip off loose ones once dry.
Keep the greens muted, use golden tufts, and lay a twig by the leaves as if a branch has fallen.

paintSteps.note: On the bare base, so any gaps still read as earth.
Over the soil once the paste is dry.
Over the grass, green mixed with bone and yellow.
Dab some leaves orange, some red and some yellow.

basing-tips.name: Asphalt road and kerb
basing-tips.summary: A dark grey road surface beside a pale cast stone kerb, grimed low down and dusty
materials: Grey acrylic texture paste
An old spatula or a scrap of plastic
A strip of plastic card for the kerb edge
Mid grey, light grey and white paints
Brown and black washes
A light clay colour for dirt
howto: Glue the kerb strip across the base, then spread texture paste either side with a spatula, not a brush.
Thin the paste with a little water near the feet, and keep the road side flatter than the kerb side.
Paint the road and the kerb as separate areas, letting each wash dry fully before any drybrush.
Wash thin brown and near black low down, along the kerb and into the cracks.
Drybrush very gently so only sharp edges catch the light, then add patches of thinned clay for dirt.

paintSteps.note: The road, with a paler grey drybrush over it.
Brown and black washes mixed, over the road.
The kerb and any cast stone slabs.
Wipe the brush almost dry, or the texture flattens.
Patches of dirt, neat in places and thinned in others.

basing-tips.name: Tundra and dry heath
basing-tips.summary: Rusty ground and pale stones with sun dried grass and a few patches of old snow
materials: Small gravel or dry dirt and a few small rocks
Thin super glue or white glue
Straw coloured tufts in mixed heights
A few small orange flower tufts
Light modelling paste for snow, if you like
A black undercoat
howto: Glue gravel and rocks down and soak them with thin glue so nothing comes loose.
Undercoat it black, drybrush heavily with a warm rusty brown, then sandy yellow, then streak grey on big stones.
Give the highest grit a light cold blue grey drybrush, as cool light on warm ground reads as chilly open land.
Glue tufts of mixed heights and drybrush any green ones pale so they look sun dried.
Add a few orange flowers for warmth and small dabs of paste for old snow, feathered at the edges.

paintSteps.note: A heavy pass over the black undercoat.
Lighter, on the raised stones.
Only the very top of the grit.
Over the tufts so the grass looks dried out.

basing-tips.name: Temple floor
basing-tips.summary: Worn sand coloured slabs carved from plaster, with a faded painted band and sand in the joints
materials: Plaster poured into a thin slab
A craft knife, a needle and a small saw
Epoxy putty and a pin
Fine sand and thinned white glue
Two bright paints and black for the pattern
A thin sepia ink
howto: Sketch the stones at base size first, then cut the slab while the plaster is still a little damp.
Score the joints with a needle, tilt a stone or two, nick the edges, then pin and glue the slab down.
Drip thinned glue into the joints, sprinkle fine sand and brush most of it away.
Paint the stones sand, then a simple band of coloured triangles on one face, outlined in black.
Scratch the pattern away at its edges, add a few fine cracks through it, then shade and drybrush.

paintSteps.note: Neat where stone meets earth.
All over the stones, skipping the earth.
Decide where the light falls before you start.
Heavy on the stone and very light over the pattern.

basing-tips.name: Skull strewn ground
basing-tips.summary: Half buried skulls in dark earth, painted along with the base and picked out last
materials: A few small plastic or resin skulls
Dried earth or fine soil
Super glue
A bone paint and a thin warm brown shade
A pale sand paint for drybrushing
Tweezers
howto: Glue the skulls in a loose cluster, some tilted and some sunk so only the top of the dome shows.
Coat the rest of the base in glue, sprinkle dried earth over it and tap off the extra.
Leave the skulls until you paint the base, so you aren't working round them twice.
Paint and drybrush the earth, then base the skulls bone and run a thinned brown shade into them.
Wipe the wash off the tops with a fingertip while wet, then pick out the domes last.

paintSteps.note: Over the ground and skulls together.
Over the earth only.
On the skulls, in thin coats.
Half water, wiped off the tops while still wet.
Bone mixed with pale grey, on the top of each skull.

basing-tips.name: Rusty metal grating
basing-tips.summary: Punched metal sheet over a dark void, with one plate lifted, worn paint and rust
materials: Thin punched metal sheet or fine mesh
Small scissors or clippers and fine sandpaper
Masking tape to protect the base rim
Super glue
Texture paste or sand for the ground below
A very matte orange paint or rust pigment
howto: Cut the sheet with small scissors or clippers and sand every cut edge, as they can be razor sharp.
Tape the rim, glue the sheet down, and cut one piece free so it can sit raised as a lifted plate.
Build some texture or a gap under the lifted plate, then undercoat it black so the void stays dark.
Sponge silver on the edges and raised pattern for worn paint, then wash grime into the holes.
Stipple very matte rust on low edges and round fixings, as rust is never shiny.

paintSteps.note: Keeps everything under the grating in shadow.
Or any old paint colour for the plates.
Dab on edges and the raised pattern for chips.
Into the holes and along the joins.
Low down and round fixings only.

basing-tips.name: Cave floor and stalagmites
basing-tips.summary: Rounded stone spikes built up from putty or clear gel, rising from a dark cave floor
materials: Two-part epoxy putty
Super glue
An old brush and a little water
Thick soft gel medium and a wide syringe, as another way
A scrap of card or plastic to build loose stones on
Photos of real caves to paint from
howto: Roll putty into balls of different sizes and fix the biggest to the base with a drop of super glue.
Press smaller balls on top into a rough spike, as soft putty sticks to itself without glue.
Brush a thin slurry of putty and water over them from top to bottom to smooth them, and repeat once dry.
Or squeeze thick gel from a syringe while lifting it slowly, building big ones in two or three dried layers.
Gel shrinks by about a third and stays a little bendy, so seal it with thin super glue before priming.

basing-tips.name: Corrupted dark forest
basing-tips.summary: Black painted twigs and tufts under cold moonlight blue, with sticky strands of rot
materials: Fine dirt or sand
Grass tufts of different heights
Small real twigs and dried sea foam plant for shrubs
Stretchy craft glue for slimy strands
Light modelling paste for drifting flecks
Cotton buds and a little alcohol
howto: Glue down dirt, then add tufts, twigs and shrubs in one varied cluster.
Once the plants are fixed, paint everything black, tufts included.
Spray or drybrush a cold pale blue from one side only, so it reads as moonlight.
Stretch strands of tacky glue between the branches so they look like rot and webbing.
Dab a few specks of light paste as drifting flecks, then clean the rim with a cotton bud dipped in alcohol.

paintSteps.note: The whole base, plants and all.
From one side only for moonlight.
A light pass to pick out texture, or use it instead of the spray.
